Mauryan Empire – socio-economic and religious conditions
Mauryan Empire – art, architecture and literature

official_questions.stem: The local name of Mohenjodaro is
official_questions.core_fact: Mohenjo-daro means 'Mound of the Dead (Men)' in Sindhi; site on the Indus in Larkana, Sindh (excavated by R.D. Banerji, 1922).

statements.t: The local name of Mohenjodaro means Mound of the Great.
The local name of Mohenjodaro means Mound of the Living.
The local name of Mohenjodaro means Mound of the Survivor.
The local name of Mohenjodaro means Mound of the Dead.

official_questions.rule: Mohenjodaro (Banerji 1922, Sindh) - Mound of the Dead; Great Bath, granary.

official_questions.stem: Name the ruler of the Kushan dynasty.
official_questions.core_fact: Kujula Kadphises (Kadphises I) founded Kushan rule in India; successors Vima Kadphises (Kadphises II), Kanishka. Ugrasena = Mahapadma Nanda; Vikramaditya = title of Chandragupta II; Pushyamitra = founder of the Sungas.

statements.t: Kadphises I was a ruler of the Kushan dynasty.
Ugrasena was a ruler of the Kushan dynasty.
statements.fact: Ugrasena is Mahapadma Nanda of the Nandas.

statements.t: Vikramaditya was a ruler of the Kushan dynasty.
Pushyamitra was a ruler of the Kushan dynasty.

official_questions.rule: Kushans: Kujula Kadphises -> Vima Takto -> Vima Kadphises -> Kanishka (78 CE, Saka era).

official_questions.stem: The title 'Vikramaditya' was assumed by
official_questions.core_fact: Chandragupta II (c. 375-415 CE) assumed the title Vikramaditya (after defeating the Shakas); Samudragupta's titles include Kaviraja and 'Indian Napoleon' (V.A. Smith).

statements.t: The title 'Vikramaditya' was assumed by Ashoka.
The title 'Vikramaditya' was assumed by Kanishka.
statements.fact: Kanishka did not take this title.

statements.t: The title 'Vikramaditya' was assumed by Samudragupta.
The title 'Vikramaditya' was assumed by Chandragupta II.

official_questions.rule: Titles: Ashoka - Devanampiya; Samudragupta - Kaviraja; Chandragupta II - Vikramaditya; Skandagupta - also Vikramaditya on coins.
official_questions.key_note: Skandagupta also used Vikramaditya; Chandragupta II is the standard answer.

official_questions.stem: The great granary of the Harappan civilisation has been found at
official_questions.core_fact: The 'Great Granary' (as named by Wheeler) is at Mohenjodaro; Harappa also has a granary complex (6+6 blocks) and Kalibangan, Lothal have storage structures.

statements.t: The great granary of the Harappan civilisation has been found at Ropar.
statements.fact: The Great Granary is at Mohenjodaro.

statements.t: The great granary of the Harappan civilisation has been found at Harappa.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Harappa has granary rows, but the 'Great Granary' is at Mohenjodaro (per key).

statements.t: The great granary of the Harappan civilisation has been found at Kalibangan.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Kalibangan is known for ploughed field/fire altars.

statements.t: The great granary of the Harappan civilisation has been found at Mohenjodaro.

official_questions.rule: Mohenjodaro: Great Bath, Great Granary; Harappa: granaries; Lothal: dockyard; Kalibangan: ploughed field.
official_questions.key_note: Some textbooks call the Harappa granary the 'Great Granary' as well; key (Mohenjodaro) retained (key of unknown status, third-party compilation).

official_questions.stem: When did Alexander invade India ?
official_questions.core_fact: Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush into north-west India in 327 BC; Battle of the Hydaspes (Porus) 326 BC; withdrew 325 BC.

statements.t: Alexander invaded India in 327 BC.
Alexander invaded India in 303 BC.
statements.fact: 303 BC is the Seleucus-Chandragupta treaty period.

statements.t: Alexander invaded India in 302 BC.
Alexander invaded India in 298 BC.

official_questions.rule: 327 BC Alexander; 326 Hydaspes; 321 Chandragupta Maurya; 305 Seleucus.

official_questions.stem: At which of the following places has a major Rock Edict of Ashoka been found ?
official_questions.core_fact: Ashoka's 14 Major Rock Edicts are at Girnar, Kalsi, Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra, Dhauli, Jaugada, Sopara, Yerragudi, Kandahar etc. Allahabad and Delhi have pillar edicts; Barabar has cave inscriptions (Ajivikas).

statements.t: A major Rock Edict of Ashoka has been found at Girnar.
A major Rock Edict of Ashoka has been found at Allahabad.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked

statements.t: A major Rock Edict of Ashoka has been found at Barabar.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked

statements.t: A major Rock Edict of Ashoka has been found at Delhi.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Delhi has pillar edicts and a minor rock edict.

official_questions.rule: Major rock edicts include Girnar, Dhauli, Jaugada, Kalsi, Erragudi (AP); pillar: Allahabad, Delhi-Topra, Lauriya, Rampurva.

official_questions.stem: Who were the immediate successors of the Mauryas in Magadha ?
official_questions.core_fact: Pushyamitra Sunga killed the last Maurya Brihadratha (c. 185 BC) and founded the Sunga dynasty in Magadha; Kanvas followed.

statements.t: The immediate successors of the Mauryas in Magadha were the Satavahanas.
The immediate successors of the Mauryas in Magadha were the Kushans.
statements.fact: Kushans came later in the NW.

statements.t: The immediate successors of the Mauryas in Magadha were the Sungas.
The immediate successors of the Mauryas in Magadha were the Pandyas.
statements.fact: Pandyas were in the far south.

official_questions.rule: Magadha: Haryanka -> Shishunaga -> Nanda -> Maurya -> Sunga -> Kanva.

official_questions.stem: The inscription, in which Asoka asked the teachers to inculcate Dharma in the minds of the students, was found at
official_questions.core_fact: Ashoka's edicts at Erragudi (Pattikonda, Kurnool) include the minor rock edict asking teachers to instil Dhamma in their pupils; Rajula Mandagiri also has a minor rock edict.

statements.t: The inscription in which Asoka asked teachers to inculcate Dharma was found at Bhattiprolu.
The inscription in which Asoka asked teachers to inculcate Dharma was found at Rajula Mandagiri.
statements.fact: Key: Erragudi (Rajula Mandagiri has a minor rock edict too).

statements.t: The inscription in which Asoka asked teachers to inculcate Dharma was found at Dhanyakataka.
The inscription in which Asoka asked teachers to inculcate Dharma was found at Erragudi.

official_questions.rule: Andhra Ashokan sites: Erragudi (major + minor), Rajula Mandagiri (minor), Amaravati pillar fragment.

official_questions.stem: Which one of the following Harappan towns has a circular arrangement of town planning ?
official_questions.core_fact: Banawali (Hissar, Haryana) shows radial streets (not the usual grid) - a 'circular/radial' arrangement.

statements.t: Mohenjodaro is the Harappan town with a circular arrangement of town planning.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked

statements.t: Lothal is the Harappan town with a circular arrangement of town planning.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Lothal has a dockyard, not a radial plan.

statements.t: Chanhudaro is the Harappan town with a circular arrangement of town planning.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Chanhudaro lacks a citadel; not radial.

statements.t: Banwali is the Harappan town with a circular arrangement of town planning.

official_questions.rule: Exceptions: Banawali radial streets; Chanhudaro no citadel; Dholavira three-part city.

official_questions.stem: Which Veda is considered as a musical treatise ?
official_questions.core_fact: The Samaveda is a collection of melodies (saman) mostly from the Rigveda, regarded as the source of Indian music.

statements.t: Rigveda is the Veda considered a musical treatise.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked

statements.t: Yajurveda is the Veda considered a musical treatise.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked

statements.t: Samaveda is the Veda considered a musical treatise.
Atharvaveda is the Veda considered a musical treatise.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked

official_questions.rule: Rig - hymns; Sama - melodies; Yajur - sacrificial formulae; Atharva - charms/medicine.

official_questions.stem: Asoka released some prisoners on humanitarian grounds on his
official_questions.core_fact: Pillar Edict V: Ashoka released prisoners on the anniversaries of his coronation (25 times in 26 years).

statements.t: Ashoka released some prisoners on humanitarian grounds on his Birthday.
Ashoka released some prisoners on humanitarian grounds on his Coronation day.
Ashoka released some prisoners on humanitarian grounds on his Conversion to Buddhism.
Ashoka released some prisoners on humanitarian grounds on his Conquest of Kalinga.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Kalinga led to remorse; prisoners released on coronation anniversaries.

official_questions.rule: PE V: release of prisoners; RE XIII: Kalinga remorse; RE II: medical care.

official_questions.stem: Fa-Hien, the Chinese traveller, visited India during the reign of
official_questions.core_fact: Fa-Hien (Faxian) visited India c. 399-411 CE during Chandragupta II's reign; Hiuen Tsang came under Harsha; Megasthenes under Chandragupta Maurya.

statements.t: Fa-Hien visited India during the reign of Chandragupta Maurya.
Fa-Hien visited India during the reign of Samudragupta.
Fa-Hien visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II.
Fa-Hien visited India during the reign of Harsha Vardhana.

official_questions.rule: Megasthenes - Chandragupta Maurya; Fa-Hien - Chandragupta II; Hiuen Tsang - Harsha.

official_questions.stem: Surya Siddhanta was written by
official_questions.core_fact: Surya Siddhanta is an anonymous astronomical text (traditionally revealed by Surya to Maya), summarised by Varahamihira in Pancha Siddhantika; Aryabhata wrote Aryabhatiya; Brahmagupta wrote Brahmasphuta Siddhanta.

statements.t: Surya Siddhanta was written by Brahmagupta.
Surya Siddhanta was written by Aryabhatta.
Surya Siddhanta was written by Varahamihira.
statements.fact: Varahamihira summarised it in Pancha Siddhantika (per key not the author).

statements.t: Surya Siddhanta was written by None of the above.

official_questions.rule: Aryabhata - Aryabhatiya; Varahamihira - Pancha Siddhantika, Brihat Samhita; Brahmagupta - Brahmasphuta Siddhanta.
official_questions.key_note: Conflict: Surya Siddhanta has no known author (often ascribed to Maya; summarised by Varahamihira); many GK sources credit Aryabhata, as the key does. 'None of the above' is arguably correct. Key retained.

official_questions.stem: Which one of the following was considered as a capital crime during the Vedic period ?
official_questions.core_fact: Vedic and later Dharmashastra texts treat brahmahatya and killing of cows as grave sins; no option is a clearly established 'capital crime' of the Vedic period.

statements.t: Murder of a person was considered a capital crime during the Vedic period.
Killing of a bull was considered a capital crime during the Vedic period.
Treachery to the king was considered a capital crime during the Vedic period.
Abortion was considered a capital crime during the Vedic period.

official_questions.rule: Vedic crimes: theft, cattle-lifting; brahmahatya worst sin in later texts.
official_questions.key_note: Deleted (cancelled) by APPSC in the final key; no reliable fact settles the options.

official_questions.stem: Which community in ancient society mostly followed Jainism ?
official_questions.core_fact: Jainism's strict ahimsa discouraged agriculture; its followers came mainly from trading/merchant communities (vaishyas).

statements.t: The community in ancient society that mostly followed Jainism was the Merchants.
The community in ancient society that mostly followed Jainism was the Artisans.
The community in ancient society that mostly followed Jainism was the Cultivators.
The community in ancient society that mostly followed Jainism was the Kshatriyas.
statements.fact: The founders were kshatriyas; followers were mainly merchants.

official_questions.rule: Jainism - merchants (no farming); Buddhism - broader (vaishyas, kings).

official_questions.stem: Which one was the backbone of the Indus economy ?
official_questions.core_fact: Agriculture (wheat, barley, cotton, surplus stored in granaries) was the backbone of the Harappan economy; trade and crafts depended on that surplus.

statements.t: The backbone of the Indus economy was Trade.
statements.fact: Trade was important; agriculture was the backbone (per key).

statements.t: The backbone of the Indus economy was Carpentry.
The backbone of the Indus economy was Cattle feeding.
The backbone of the Indus economy was Agriculture.

official_questions.rule: Harappan: agriculture base; trade with Mesopotamia (Meluhha); first to grow cotton.
official_questions.key_note: APPSC's corrected final key is Agriculture; trade is sometimes cited as the 'backbone' in GK books.

official_questions.stem: The decline of trade and commerce in North India between 7th and 10th centuries was partly due to the
options: Decline in skills of Indian artisans
official_questions.core_fact: In R.S. Sharma's 'Indian feudalism' view, long-distance trade and towns declined in North India c. 600-1000 AD, partly because the collapse of the Western Roman Empire (5th c.) ended the Roman trade.

statements.t: The decline of trade and commerce in North India between the 7th and 10th centuries was partly due to the Collapse of West Roman Empire.
The decline of trade and commerce in North India between the 7th and 10th centuries was partly due to the Collapse of China.
statements.fact: China under the Tang (618-907) flourished; it did not collapse.

statements.t: The decline of trade and commerce in North India between the 7th and 10th centuries was partly due to the Collapse of South East Asia.
statements.fact: South-East Asian trade (Srivijaya) grew in this period.

statements.t: The decline of trade and commerce in North India between the 7th and 10th centuries was partly due to the Decline in skills of Indian artisans.
statements.d: Decline in skills of Indian artisans
statements.fact: Decline is attributed to loss of markets, not of artisan skills.

official_questions.rule: Post-Gupta decline: fall of the Western Roman Empire, Huna invasions, land grants and self-sufficient villages (R.S. Sharma).

official_questions.stem: 'Anda, harmika and chhatri' are integral parts of which one of the following Buddhist monuments ?
official_questions.core_fact: A stupa has the anda (hemispherical dome), harmika (railed square on top) and chhatri (umbrella on the yasti), plus medhi, vedika and toranas.

statements.t: Anda, harmika and chhatri are integral parts of Chaityas.
statements.fact: Chaityas are prayer halls; anda/harmika/chhatri belong to stupas (a small stupa sits inside a chaitya).

statements.t: Anda, harmika and chhatri are integral parts of Viharas.
Anda, harmika and chhatri are integral parts of Stupas.
Anda, harmika and chhatri are integral parts of Basadis.

official_questions.rule: Stupa parts: anda, harmika, chhatri, yasti, medhi, vedika, torana; chaitya = hall; vihara = monastery.

official_questions.stem: Which of the following is not a Harappan site ?
official_questions.core_fact: Sutkagendor (Baluchistan), Surkotada (Kutch) and Rakhigarhi (Haryana) are Harappan sites; Sohgaura (Gorakhpur) is known for a Mauryan-period copper plate inscription.

statements.t: Sutkagendor is not a Harappan site.
statements.fact: Sutkagendor is a Harappan site (Makran coast).

statements.t: Surkotada is not a Harappan site.
Sohgaura is not a Harappan site.
Rakhigarhi is not a Harappan site.

official_questions.rule: Harappan: Sutkagendor, Surkotada, Rakhigarhi, Dholavira; Sohgaura & Mahasthan = Mauryan famine-relief inscriptions.

official_questions.stem: Which of the following inscriptions mentions the names of Vedic Gods Indra, Varuna, Mitra and Nasatyas ?
official_questions.core_fact: The Boghazkoi (Hattusa, Turkey) inscription, c. 1380 BC, a Hittite-Mitanni treaty, invokes Indra, Varuna, Mitra and the Nasatyas – early evidence of Rigvedic gods outside India.

statements.t: The Mansehra inscription mentions the Vedic gods Indra, Varuna, Mitra and Nasatyas.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Mansehra carries Ashoka's rock edicts, not Vedic gods.

statements.t: The Shahbazgarhi inscription mentions the Vedic gods Indra, Varuna, Mitra and Nasatyas.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked

statements.t: The Boghazkoi inscription mentions the Vedic gods Indra, Varuna, Mitra and Nasatyas.
The Junagarh inscription mentions the Vedic gods Indra, Varuna, Mitra and Nasatyas.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Junagarh has Ashoka's edicts and Rudradaman's inscription on Sudarshana lake.

official_questions.rule: Boghazkoi (c. 1400 BC, Anatolia) = Vedic gods; Mansehra/Shahbazgarhi = Kharosthi Ashokan edicts; Junagarh = Rudradaman (first long Sanskrit inscription).

official_questions.stem: Which among the following pillar inscriptions of Ashoka states that the land revenue rate of Lumbini was reduced to one-eighth ?
official_questions.core_fact: Ashoka's Rummindei (Lumbini) pillar inscription records his visit in the 20th regnal year, exemption from bali and reduction of bhaga to one-eighth.

statements.t: The Maski pillar inscription states that the land revenue of Lumbini was reduced to one-eighth.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Maski is a minor rock edict (first with the name Asoka), not a pillar.

statements.t: The Rummindei pillar inscription states that the land revenue of Lumbini was reduced to one-eighth.
The Kalsi pillar inscription states that the land revenue of Lumbini was reduced to one-eighth.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Kalsi has the major rock edicts.

statements.t: The Vaishali pillar inscription states that the land revenue of Lumbini was reduced to one-eighth.
statements.fact: Vaishali pillar has no Ashokan edict on Lumbini.

official_questions.rule: Rummindei: bali exempt, bhaga 1/8; Maski/Gujarra: name 'Asoka'; Kalsi: major rock edicts.

official_questions.stem: Which Mauryan officer was the incharge of Weights and Measures ?
official_questions.core_fact: Kautilya's Arthashastra names the Pautavadhyaksha as superintendent of weights and measures.

statements.t: The Mauryan officer in charge of weights and measures was the Sulkadhyaksha.
The Mauryan officer in charge of weights and measures was the Samsthadhyaksha.
The Mauryan officer in charge of weights and measures was the Pautavadhyaksha.
The Mauryan officer in charge of weights and measures was the Panyadhyaksha.

official_questions.rule: Adhyakshas: Pautava = weights; Sulka = tolls; Panya = commerce; Sita = crown land; Suradhyaksha = liquor; Navadhyaksha = ships.

official_questions.stem: Romaka Siddhanta written by Varahamihira deals with :
official_questions.core_fact: The Romaka Siddhanta, summarised in Varahamihira's Panchasiddhantika, is an astronomical text (based on Greco-Roman astronomy).

statements.t: Romaka Siddhanta written by Varahamihira deals with Chemistry.
Romaka Siddhanta written by Varahamihira deals with Mathematics.
statements.fact: Its subject is astronomy (with mathematical computation).

statements.t: Romaka Siddhanta written by Varahamihira deals with Astronomy.
Romaka Siddhanta written by Varahamihira deals with Medicine.

official_questions.rule: Varahamihira: Panchasiddhantika (5 siddhantas incl. Romaka, Paulisa), Brihat Samhita, Brihat Jataka.
official_questions.key_note: Strictly, Varahamihira summarised the Romaka Siddhanta in his Panchasiddhantika; key kept.

official_questions.stem: Which one of the following books was not written by Harshavardhana ?
official_questions.core_fact: Harsha wrote the Sanskrit plays Priyadarshika, Ratnavali and Nagananda; Kadambari is Banabhatta's prose romance.

statements.t: Priyadarshika was not written by Harshavardhana.
Ratnavali was not written by Harshavardhana.
Nagananda was not written by Harshavardhana.
Kadambari was not written by Harshavardhana.

official_questions.rule: Harsha: Ratnavali, Priyadarshika, Nagananda; Bana: Harshacharita, Kadambari.

official_questions.stem: Which religion did King Kharavela patronise ?
official_questions.core_fact: Kharavela of Kalinga (c. 1st c. BCE) was a Jain patron; Hathigumpha inscription, Udayagiri caves.

statements.t: King Kharavela patronised Jainism.
King Kharavela patronised Buddhism.
King Kharavela patronised Shaivism.
King Kharavela patronised Vaishnavism.

official_questions.rule: Kharavela = Jain; contemporary of Satakarni I.
